title: The one who prostrates
hookLine: Ali Zayn al-Abidin, who survived Karbala, leaves prayers gathered in al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya

cards: The boy Zaynab shielded in Kufa lived. He was Ali, Husayn's son, too sick on the day of Karbala to fight, and he grew into a man who went back to Medina. He did not raise an army.

He did not make speeches against the palace in Damascus. What people remembered about him was quieter and stranger: how often, and how long, he lay with his forehead on the ground. They gave him names for it.
Zayn al-Abidin, the ornament of the worshippers. And al-Sajjad.

teach.h: SUJUD: THE FOREHEAD ON THE GROUND.
teach.b: Al-Sajjad is tied to sujud, the prostration of prayer, when the forehead touches the ground. Tradition explains the name as one who does it again and again: the one of prostrations.
For Shia Muslims, Ali Zayn al-Abidin is the fourth Imam. Sunni scholars honored him too; the hadith scholar al-Zuhri, who knew him in Medina, is reported to have praised him warmly.
He left a book of prayers, al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya, the pages of al-Sajjad, treasured in Shia tradition as words of an Imam addressed to God. The range is wide.

Prayers for the morning and the evening, for the new moon, for the coming of Ramadan. A prayer for his parents, asking that he might be gentle with them and lower his voice before them. A prayer for his children.
A prayer for his neighbors and friends, asking for the grace to visit the sick among them, to give without being asked, to cover their faults. Even a prayer for the soldiers guarding the frontiers.
A man who had lost his father and brothers at Karbala prays for ordinary people's kitchens and doorsteps. Tradition adds a story told about him by Sunni and Shia writers alike.

teach.h: BREAD AT THE DOOR BY NIGHT.
teach.b: Families in Medina found sacks of bread at their doors by night and never knew from whom.
When he died, the bread stopped, and those who washed his body found marks on his back from carrying it. Whatever grief he carried, he turned it into prostration, and into bread.

how: Shia Muslims read the supplications of al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya, the prayers of the fourth Imam, privately and in gatherings, often on particular days and occasions the prayers themselves name.

o: a prayer rug kept for prostration in prayer
the one who calls the faithful to prayer
the one who prostrates often, Husayn's son

games.q: the one who prostrates — tap the pairs.

s: the Sahifa's prayers are only about grief for Karbala
it has prayers for parents, children, neighbors, the new moon, Ramadan and more.
Ali Zayn al-Abidin was the boy Zaynab shielded in Kufa
too sick to fight at Karbala, he lived and returned to Medina.
he led a revolt against Damascus
what people remembered was his prayer, and bread left at doors by night.

games.q: you survived Karbala and came home to Medina. how do you carry it?
o: raise an army to avenge your father.
pray, and quietly feed the poor by night.
leave Medina and never speak of it.
games.why: he became known for long prostrations, and tradition says families found bread at their doors by night, from him.

practice: Take what his prayer for neighbors asks and hold it: visit the sick, give before being asked, cover a fault instead of exposing it. Bring one neighbor to mind, and ask which of those three you might offer them.
If you pray, you can bow your head, or put your forehead to the ground.

wordCard.voice: Al-Sajjad, the one who prostrates often: Ali Zayn al-Abidin, who survived Karbala and left the prayers gathered in al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the one who prostrates often, from sujud, prostration.

carryVoice: Your line: the one of prostrations. Quiet kindness, left unsigned, like bread at a door. See you tomorrow.
